subject: Follow-up: Reliability & SLO comparison vs Hyperscaler — next tests & asks

Subject: Reliability & SLO follow-up — Redwood vs Hyperscalers

Hi Alex —

Thanks again for the call today. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we can make the competitive evaluation tangible: 

Recap from discovery:
- Primary success metric: <99.95% uptime per month with meaningful error-budget policies for business-critical customer flows.
- Peak QPS target: 1k sustained, 3k short bursts.
- Failover expectations: graceful regional failover with <500ms additional tail latency ideally; clear behavior on rate-limits.
- Security/compliance: SOC2 evidence requested in a follow-up (we covered at a high level).

What we propose as tests:
1) 24-hour sustained ramp test — measure throughput, p50/p90/p99 latencies, error rates.
2) Rate-limit & burst test — characterise rate limiting behavior and soft/hard limits.
3) Failover simulation — route traffic to a secondary region and measure recovery/consistency and error-surface.
4) Long-tail error budget calculation — we’ll provide logs and a proposed calculation template.

Attached: SLO comparison (Redwood vs typical hyperscaler-hosted endpoints) and a short deployment guide for the Private/ Dedicated variants.

Asks from your side:
- Confirm the acceptance criteria for the 24-hour test (what does Acme consider "acceptable" error budget burn?).
- Share a contact for your infra/ops who can run/observe the test (or we can run tests and share dashboards).
- Preferred time window next week for running the 24-hour test.

I'll loop Marissa (CS) and Aditya (SE) on the technical plan after you confirm so we can schedule and share a test plan link.

Thanks,
Ben

Alex —

Great, appreciate the fast turnaround. Quick answers inline and next steps below.

- Error budget window: by default we compute both 30- and 90-day rolling windows in our dashboards; for the test we can publish both, but recommend 30-day for initial acceptance criteria. We'll share the exact calculation template (attached in the shared test doc).

- Rate limits/fail-open behavior: Redwood supports configurable soft and hard rate limits per API key + per-route. Typical behavior: soft limit triggers 429 warnings with explanatory headers and optional backoff guidance; hard limit results in 429s. For Dedicated/Private deployments we can implement queuing or token-bucket shaping at the ingress if you prefer — that'll be part of the deployment config. We do not silently fall back to lower-tier models by default unless configured as an explicit routing policy.

- Failover patterns: we support both warm-standby and active-active. Active-active provides faster recovery but higher cost; warm-standby reduces cost and gives deterministic failover behavior that we can sweep for your acceptance tests. We'll include cost delta estimates in the test plan.

Next steps:
1) Marissa will propose an exact test plan and SLO acceptance template.
2) Aditya will work with Tom on the test orchestration (IP ranges, load-generator config, credentials).
3) Ben/Marissa to share dashboard access and a 24-hour monitoring link during the run.

Marissa / Aditya — can you confirm availability Apr 6–7 afternoon PT to run the test and who on the Redwood side will be on-call for the run?

Thanks,
Ben

Hi Alex / Ben —

I'll own the test plan and SLO acceptance template. High-level notes for Acme's evaluation vs typical hyperscaler-managed endpoints: 

SLOs & metrics we'll publish during the test:
- Uptime (successful 2xx responses / total requests) — computed over 30d and 90d rolling windows.
- Latency percentiles: p50 / p90 / p99 for request-to-first-byte and full-response.
- Error budget burn: detailed events (5xx spikes, 429 spikes) with timestamps; we include a burn-rate heatmap.
- Rate limiting behaviour: headers returned (X-RateLimit-Remaining, Retry-After), and whether backpressure results in queueing or reject.
- Failover observability: health-check timeline, routing changes, and KV cache warmup metrics (since large LLMs can show tail effects on cold caches).

Acceptance suggestions (for discussion):
- Uptime: >= 99.95% over test window (30d equivalent) with no single incident > 1% of monthly error budget.
- Rate limits: graceful throttling with >=95% of requests receiving Retry-After header and clear 429 semantics.
- Failover: Active-active preferred for customer-facing flows; if warm-standby used, failover should restore to <2x p99 latency within 5 minutes.

Operational notes for the run:
- We'll provide a dedicated API key and a limited cluster to run the tests.
- For Dedicated/Private evaluations we recommend running the failover test across two regions (us-west-2 <-> us-east-1) to show cross-region routing and KV cache behavior.
- We'll provision a Grafana dashboard + a shared log link (we'll give access to Tom).

Deliverables after the run:
- Test report with raw metrics, SLO calculation, incident timeline, and recommendations (quantized cost delta for active-active vs warm-standby).
- A short runbook for how Acme can maintain the SLOs in production (autoscale knobs, batching configs, cache advice).

I can be on-call for Apr 6 afternoon PT — Aditya, can you confirm you'll own test orchestration and IP whitelisting?

Best,
